title: Working as Part of a Team
summary: Learn how effective teams coordinate individual responsibilities, share information, depend on one another, and work toward a common result without losing individual accountability.
objectives: Explain the difference between being in a group and functioning as a team.
Identify how individual work contributes to a shared result.
Recognize the importance of coordination, reliability, role boundaries, and shared goals.

vocab.def: Coordinated work in which people contribute different responsibilities toward a shared result.
Working with other people by sharing information, ideas, decisions, or responsibilities appropriately.
A result that multiple people or roles are working together to achieve.
A relationship in which one task, person, or team relies on another task or result.

sections.heading: A team is more than a group of people
sections.body: People become a working team when their responsibilities connect to a shared result. Simply being in the same room, department, class, or project does not automatically create effective teamwork.

sections.heading: Individual work affects the whole team
sections.body: A team may depend on each person completing different work. When one task is late, incomplete, unsafe, or inaccurate, other people may be unable to continue their own responsibilities.

sections.heading: Teamwork does not erase individual accountability
sections.body: A team result does not prove that every member made the same contribution. Each person remains responsible for the work, decisions, communication, and commitments that belong to them.

sections.heading: Strong teams coordinate instead of guessing
sections.body: Effective teams make responsibilities, dependencies, status, and next steps visible. When something changes, team members communicate early enough for others to adjust.

practice.prompt: Your work must be completed before another teammate can begin their part. You realize you will be late. What should you do?
practice.answer: Communicate the delay early, explain the current status, and identify how the dependency may affect the next person's work.

practice.prompt: A team project succeeds, but one person did not complete their assigned responsibility. Does the team result automatically prove that person's contribution?
practice.answer: No. Team membership or team success does not by itself prove an individual's contribution.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes effective workplace teamwork?
options: People coordinate individual responsibilities toward a shared result
Everyone performs the same task in the same way
Individual responsibilities no longer matter once people join a team
Team members should avoid discussing delays or dependencies
quiz.answer: People coordinate individual responsibilities toward a shared result

lab.objective: Map a simple team project by identifying the shared goal, each person's responsibility, important dependencies, and where status updates or handoffs are needed.

reflectionPrompt: Describe one way your individual reliability can affect another person on a team.
